newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians gear up for general election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians gear up for general election campaign.

text.p: Indonesia's three legal political parties start a month-long general election campaign on Sunday, with leaders calling for restraint to prevent violence that has caused jitters on financial markets.
Political and military officials, including President Suharto and armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung, have stressed the need for calm during the campaign period leading up to the May 29 vote.
Golkar, the ruling party since Suharto took power 30 years ago, is looking for just over 70 percent of the vote from the 124.7 million electorate.
It won 68 percent in the last election in 1992, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 17 percent and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) 15 percent.
The three parties are the only political groups legally entitled to contest the national and local elections.

The elections will be going on without the participation of Indonesia's best-known opposition politician Megawati Sukarnoputri, the one-time PDI leader ousted by government-backed rebels in June last year.

The official electoral commission refused to accept her candidates for the polls, and she has called on her supporters to boycott the campaign at least partly to avoid violence -- a move in fact welcomed by the government. She avoided calling for an illegal boycott of the vote itself.

Golkar has said it will push government development policies ranging from agriculture and industry to social welfare in the campaign through the sprawling tropical archipelago of more than 17,000 islands.
The PPP says its campaign theme is "justice", and the PDI says it seeks to promote democracy, social justice and the spirit of nationalism.

But political analysts say the elections for the 500-seat House of Representatives are really a preliminary to a presidential poll in March next year when Suharto is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term in office.

Analysts say the key political question facing the nation of 200 million people is who he will select as his running mate, and how the 75-year-old leader will approach the issue of an eventual successor.
Concern over posible violence during the general election campaign hit the rupiah during the past week. It dropped 20 points to 2,440.50 to the dollar before moving back to 2,436 by Saturday.
The Jakarta Stock Exchange was little changed on Friday, with the composite index closing at 652.4 points, but brokers attributed some profit-taking to election jitters.

"The crucial point is Sunday and Monday. People are looking at the start of the campaign which should give indications whether the authorities have things under control," a foreign exchange dealer said on Friday.
But economic analysts said the economy was fundamentally sound despite market concerns over the political situation.
Brokers contacted at the weekend anticipated the stock index would rise to between 750 and 800 points by the end of the year.
Economists and currency dealers were also optimistic on the outlook for the rupiah.
"There will be a lot of volatility in the next few weeks. But the rupiah will recover after that," Trisiladi Supriyanto, vice-president of Bank of America in Jakarta, told Reuters.

Analysts said the May 29 voting for the 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives -- the other 75 are alloted to the military which does not vote -- could give some indication of the relative strengths and weaknesses for contenders for the vice-presidential post next year.

Analysts said they would also be looking at the relative percentage changes in the fortunes of the three parties, and the size of a protest vote by blanking all three parties, or by just staying away from the polls.
